records_and_firsts: The LPC called part of the house the oldest surviving building in the city at the time of designation.
cultural_history: The first portion is usually dated to about 1652. Later rooms and modifications account for much of the building visible today.
fun_facts: It was the subject of LPC's first individual landmark designation in 1965.
The federal landmark survey describes the earliest wall framing as filled with wattle and daub, a woven lattice coated with an earthen mixture. The later additions used brick infill.
visual_identifiers: Low, broad rooflines and visible additions are more useful for recognition than a single date or style.
Look at how the lower edge of the steep roof flares outward over the shingled walls.

significance.reason: A surviving seventeenth-century Dutch colonial house core and the first LPC designation.

evidence.locator: Section 7, description of the roof and walls

chronology.description: Dismantling began in 1963. By late 1966 the headhouse was gone.

cultural_history: Municipal Archives records reveal preservation negotiations around the demolition and proposals for retaining architectural pieces.
McKim, Mead & White drew on Rome’s Baths of Caracalla for the station’s grand waiting room. The station organized passengers, trains, and street traffic on separate levels.
visual_identifiers: In interior photographs, the main waiting room has a heavy coffered vault. The train concourse is recognizable by its tall glazed roof and open steel framing.
viewing: The current arena and tower occupy the old station site. Date-stamped station images should distinguish the removed headhouse from the surviving railway approaches.

relationships.description: The replacement station continued passenger service after the original aboveground headhouse was demolished.
The present arena was built above the replacement station.
Two Penn Plaza was part of the successor site development.

significance.reason: Saarinen's vaulted terminal forms a recognizable work of expressive concrete and survives through adaptive reuse.

cultural_history: The house's layers include a Dutch colonial core and later changes to its domestic appearance. Alice Austen's family acquired it in the nineteenth century.
fun_facts: Austen documented street life and intimate social settings through a photography practice closely associated with this waterfront home.
Alice Austen developed her photographs in a second-floor darkroom at Clear Comfort and rinsed them at the pump behind the house.
visual_identifiers: At the waterfront, look for the Gothic Revival additions, including the decorative wood trim along the gables and the projecting bay window.
viewing: The harbor-facing setting provides a ground-level reference point on the Staten Island side of the Narrows.

significance.reason: The harbor-facing home of photographer Alice Austen preserves an important cultural association.
